name: Photo lighting / golden hour
lead: Photo lighting is the choice of light used when a face is photographed, and golden hour is the best-known version: the period shortly after sunrise or before sunset when daylight is redder and softer than at midday [1]. People use it to look better in photos, because low-contrast, warm light leaves shadows less dark and highlights less likely to blow out, which makes skin and facial features read more evenly [1].

Portrait photographers have long managed light for this purpose. Nineteenth-century sitters were lit by soft overhead window light, a window and a reflector are described as enough for amateurs and professionals, and a white reflector bounces light into the darker side of the face to even out contrast [2]. Midday sun produces strong highlights and dark shadows that portrait photographers often offset with fill flash [1].

The same logic runs through the rest of portrait lighting: the size, distance and direction of the main light decide which parts of a face are emphasised and how deep the shadows under the brow, nose and jaw fall [3][4]. Named patterns such as loop, butterfly, split and Rembrandt lighting are shorthand for where the key light sits [3][6], and ring lights, softboxes and reflectors are common tools for softening or filling shadows [5][7].

In looksmaxxing and photo-presentation circles, soft window, shade or evening light is a common way to improve dating-profile and social photos without changing the face. No studies were found that test lighting choice against perceived attractiveness.

paras: When the sun is low its rays cross more atmosphere, which weakens direct light. More of the illumination then comes from indirect skylight, lowering the lighting ratio, and more blue light is scattered so the sun looks reddish [1]. Contrast is lower, so shadows are less dark and highlights less likely to be overexposed, and the low angle produces longer shadows [1].

Colour temperature is roughly 2,000 K near sunrise or sunset, about 3,500 K during the golden hour and about 5,500 K at midday, with altitude, latitude, season and weather shifting these values [1]. The 'hour' is figurative. Its length varies with season and latitude, and planning tools define it by sun altitude, for example 0 to 6 or 0 to 10 degrees above the horizon [1]. Cinematographer Nestor Almendros described the related 'magic hour' on Days of Heaven as lasting about twenty minutes a day [1]. The blue hour just before sunrise or after sunset has mostly blue light and no sharp shadows [1].

Soft light is diffused and seems to wrap around a subject, casting shadows with soft edges, while hard light comes from a single small, bright source and produces high contrast and sharply defined shadows [7]. Hardness depends on the size of the source, its distance from the subject and the thickness of any diffusion [7]. Wikipedia lists larger sources, closer placement, softboxes, diffusion gel or silk, reflectors and cloud cover as ways to soften light, and says soft light is popular because it diffuses hard shadows and produces more flattering images of the human form [7]. Hard light, by contrast, accentuates texture and gives a stronger sense of three-dimensionality [7].
For a face this means an overcast sky, open shade, a north-facing window or a diffused lamp all act as large soft sources, whereas direct overhead sun or a bare small flash acts as a hard one [1][7].

Window light has been used for portraits for decades; early morning and late afternoon are described as the best times, and curtains, reflectors and shields soften it [2]. In studio setups the key light sits roughly 30 to 60 degrees from the camera, a fill light or reflector opposite it reduces shadows, and softboxes give softer light than open strobes [2].

In classic three-point lighting the key light sits 30 to 45 degrees to one side of the camera axis and 30 to 45 degrees above it, a fill on the opposite side lightens shadows such as the nose shadow, often at up to half the key's brightness, and a back light outlines the hair and shoulders [4]. Too much fill makes an image flat and low in contrast [4].

Named patterns describe where the key sits: loop lighting leaves a small nose shadow on the shadowed cheek, butterfly lighting places the light above and in line with the camera to make a butterfly-shaped shadow under the nose, split lighting comes from about 90 degrees to the side, and Rembrandt lighting comes high and to the side to leave a lit patch on the far cheek [3]. Butterfly lighting, with the key above the camera and fill below, was a favourite of Hollywood portraitist George Hurrell and is also called Paramount lighting [2]. High-key lighting gives a mostly shadow-free image, while low-key lighting produces dark shadows [2].

The Rembrandt look is defined by a small lit triangle under the eye on the shadowed side of the face, which Wikipedia says should be no longer than the nose and no wider than the eye [6]. It can be made with one light and a reflector, with fill at roughly half the key's power, and moving the lights or changing the key-to-fill balance makes it subtler or more dramatic [6]. Director Cecil B. DeMille is credited with first using the term on The Warrens of Virginia (1915), and the style is common in film noir [6].

A ring flash surrounds the lens so that light falls evenly around the optical axis, minimising shadows and producing circular catchlights in the eyes; Lester A. Dine invented it in 1952 for dental photography [5]. Continuous LED ring lights became popular for video calls, selfies and vlogging, with use growing during the COVID-19 pandemic partly because of TikTok, and typically sell for $10 to $100 [5]. Wikipedia says makeup artists often use them and that photographers use ring flash for portraits and fashion for its softened shadows and eye highlights [5].

Appearance communities discuss photo lighting alongside angles, lenses and editing as part of presenting the face well in profile pictures. Proponents say soft directional light reduces harsh shadows under the eyes and along the jaw, and that midday overhead sun does the opposite. These are practitioner views; the sources cited here describe the lighting effects in general terms rather than for faces specifically.

Photographers on the T Nation forum, discussing food and landscape shots, mention the same basic rules, such as shooting within an hour of sunrise or sunset and avoiding the flat light of noon.[8][9] Lighting is also a free way to change a photo: it requires only choosing the time, the window and the position of the subject, whereas surgical or cosmetic routes change the face itself.

timeline.event: Cecil B. DeMille is credited with first using the term Rembrandt lighting while shooting The Warrens of Virginia.[6]
Lester A. Dine invents the ring flash for dental photography.[5]
Days of Heaven is shot largely in the 'magic hour'; Nestor Almendros wins an Academy Award for it.[1]
Ring lights surge in popularity for video calls and selfies during the COVID-19 pandemic, partly because of TikTok.[5]

lore.intro: Soft or golden light is a recurring suggestion in photo-presentation advice.

claims.claim: Soft golden-hour light makes faces look better in photos
claims.believers: Proponents say low, warm light softens shadows and skin texture, so the face photographs more evenly.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports lower contrast, less dark shadows and fewer blown highlights at golden hour, and notes it is often preferred for portraits [1]. No published study has tested the effect on perceived attractiveness.

claims.believers: Photographers and users say strong overhead light creates harsh shadows.
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes midday sun creates strong highlights and dark shadows that portrait photographers often counter with fill flash [1].

claims.claim: A big soft light source flatters more than a small hard one
claims.believers: Photographers say softboxes, windows and overcast skies wrap light around the face and soften skin texture.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says soft light is popular for producing more flattering images of the human form, and that hard light emphasises texture.[7] No published study has tested this against attractiveness ratings.

claims.claim: Ring lights give a clean selfie look
claims.believers: Creators and makeup artists use ring lights for even, shadowless light and eye catchlights.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the shadow-minimising design and catchlights; no study has compared ring lights with other setups for attractiveness.[5]

claims.claim: Light from above and slightly to the side shapes the cheekbones
claims.believers: Rembrandt, loop and butterfly patterns are used to add shadow beneath cheekbones and define the face.[3][6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the patterns and where the key light sits; the effect on perceived attractiveness is unmeasured.[3][6]

claims.claim: Fill light or a reflector evens out shadows under the eyes
claims.believers: Portraitists use a white reflector or fill light opposite the key to lift darker areas of the face.[2][4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes fill lightens shadows from the key but that too much makes an image flat.[4]

card.summary: Shooting in soft, low-angle light to flatter your face on camera; physics is clear, the attractiveness payoff is untested.

quick.overview:
Golden hour is the soft, warm light near sunrise and sunset. Photographers favour it for portraits because it lowers contrast and softens shadows.

Whether it makes people look more attractive in photos has not been studied.
quick.mechanism: Low sun passes through more atmosphere, so light is warmer and more diffuse, with gentler shadows.[1]
quick.risks: No health risks. The only caveat is that effects on perceived attractiveness are unmeasured.

chain: Low sun or diffused window light lowers contrast
Shadows under the brow, eyes and jaw are softer
Face looks more even and flattering in the photo
angle.text: Choosing soft, low-angle or diffused light changes how a face is rendered in a photo: shadows are lighter and highlights less harsh [1][2]. People apply it to profile and social photos to present their features at their best.
